The Spirituality of Muslim Women:
Voices, Scholarship & Leadership

A visual and scholarly exploration of Muslim women's contributions to Islamic civilization from the sacred cities of Mecca to contemporary media, politics, and Qur'anic scholarship.

إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَالْمُسْلِمَاتِ وَالْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ وَالْقَانِتِينَ وَالْقَانِتَاتِ...
"Surely for Muslim men and women, believing men and women, devout men and women, truthful men and women, patient men and women, humble men and women, charitable men and women, fasting men and women, men and women who guard their chastity, and men and women who remember Allah often for all of them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward."

Qur'an, Surat Al-Ahzab 33:35

Original collage RelStud/IslamStu 3131B, Spirituality of Muslim Women, Huron University 2025

Project overview

What a Picture Alone Cannot Tell You

This project is a collage that integrates course themes such as hadith scholarship, Qur'anic address of Muslim women, and political leadership into a single visual that honours the rich, diverse, and often overlooked tradition of Muslim women across history and into the contemporary world.

When asked what a picture really tells you about someone, the answer is: on its own, not enough. A photograph conveys a face and a name it cannot tell you a story, a scholarly argument, or a historical context. This website transforms the collage from a classroom submission into a public educational resource, making each image a symbol of each woman's contribution and the website a platform to learn more about the artwork.

The target audience is intentionally broad: anyone interested in learning more about Muslim women and their contributions to Islamic civilization Muslim students who may never have been taught that women narrated hadith, non-Muslim Canadians encountering these figures for the first time, and scholars seeking connections between historical and contemporary Muslim women's leadership.

01
Recognition
Muslim women's contributions to Islamic civilization are historically deep, geographically diverse, and ongoing not marginal or past.
02
Disruption
Religious scholarship, political leadership, and public media are not exclusively male domains and never have been.
03
Framework
A new way of reading Islamic history: one that centres women's agency rather than treating it as an exception or afterthought.

Qur'anic anchor: The centre of this piece is verse 35 from Surah Al-Ahzab. As classical sources such as Musnad Ahmad record, while Umm Salamah was combing her hair, she heard the Prophet reciting from the pulpit and asked him why the Qur'an did not name women as it named men. This verse was revealed shortly after as a direct response encoding a woman's voice into the very mechanism of revelation.

The women in the collage

Sacred Cities, Scholars, Activists & Contemporary Leaders

Hajar (Hagar)
Matriarch of Mecca | The Well of Zamzam, Foundation of Mecca
Sacred Cities & Matriarchs

The Well of Zamzam and the images of pilgrims around the hill of Safa symbolize Hajar, the wife of Prophet Ibrahim and mother of Prophet Ismail. Her journey of Sa'i running between Safa and Marwa in search of water is commemorated as a mandatory ritual for both men and women in one of Islam's Five Pillars to this day.

Including Hajar asserts that Muslim women's foundational contributions to Islamic civilization predate the Prophet Muhammad and are woven into the compulsory practice of every Muslim who undertakes Hajj. One of the most physically central rituals in Islam literally re-enacts the actions of a woman.

Khoja Ismail, Sakina Hassan & Munira Abdu
Egypt, 20th century
Female Reciters

Pioneering female reciters and shaikhas who broke through the barriers of the Cairo Qur'an Radio Station, facing significant public backlash. Their inclusion challenges the assumption that religious vocal authority is an exclusively male domain in Islam.

As Shaker (2023) documents in New Lines Magazine, these women navigated sustained institutional and public resistance simply for reciting the Qur'an on air a form of religious authority that had long been coded as male.

Summaya Al-Deeb
Egypt
Female Reciter

One of the shaikhas featured in the collage who broke through the barriers of the Cairo Qur'an Radio Station. Her recitation challenged the gendering of religious vocal authority in Egypt's most prominent Qur'anic broadcasting institution.

Muhammad Akram Nadwi
Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies
Hadith Scholarship

Compiled a 43-volume encyclopedia (Al-Wafā' bi-asmā' al-nisā') documenting over 10,000 female hadith narrators, affirming that women's scholarly tradition is foundational to Islamic knowledge transmission.

Significantly, Nadwi himself expressed frustration that even after male students encountered his findings, some continued to ignore or dismiss women's contributions suggesting the barrier is not merely lack of education but a deeper resistance to revising assumptions about religious authority (I. Mattson, personal communication, 2025).

10,000+
female hadith narrators documented a tradition long marginalized in mainstream Islamic education
Zainab Al-Ghazali
Egypt, 1917 2005
Activist & Author

A prominent Egyptian Muslim activist whose autobiography Days from My Life documents her imprisonment under Gamal Abdel Nasser's regime in the 1960s. The collage includes her book cover paired with an image of a hand behind prison bars, symbolizing her courage and endurance.

Her prison writings analysed by Essa Said (2025) fit within a broader tradition of Arab women's incarceration literature that asserts political voice through literary form.

Benazir Bhutto
Pakistan, 1953 2007
Political Leader

The first woman elected to lead a democratic government in a Muslim-majority country, serving as Prime Minister of Pakistan. The collage includes her book Reconciliation: Islam, Democracy, and the West (2008), in which Bhutto argues that Islam and democratic governance are compatible a position directly relevant to course debates on Muslim women in political leadership.

Houda Al-Habash
Syria
Education & Leadership

Founder of a girls' Qur'an school in Damascus and subject of the documentary The Light in Her Eyes (Meltzer et al., 2011). Al-Habash built an institution where girls receive rigorous Qur'anic education, arguing through practice that Islamic learning for women is a priority, not an afterthought.

Zarqa Nawaz
Canada
Literature & Humour

Author of Laughing All the Way to the Mosque (2015) and creator of CBC's Little Mosque on the Prairie. Nawaz humanizes Muslim women through comedy, arguing implicitly that humour is itself a form of agency refusing the sombreness often imposed on Muslim women's public presence.

Ginella Massa
Canada, b. 1985
Media & Representation

First hijab-wearing television news anchor in North America, making history at CityNews Toronto in November 2016. Her presence on air challenged racialized and gendered assumptions about who belongs in North American newsrooms in Canada, not in a distant context.

Massa serves as an accessible entry point for a North American audience: a familiar face that draws viewers into the less familiar stories of the Cairo reciters, Nadwi's encyclopedia, and Umm Salamah's role in the revelation of 33:35.

Ibtihaj Muhammad
United States, b. 1985
Sport & Representation

First American Muslim woman to compete and win an Olympic medal while wearing a hijab, at the 2016 Rio Olympics. The National Women's History Museum (Brandman, 2021) notes how Muhammad's visibility transformed the public image of Muslim women in American sport under the American flag.

Her inclusion insists that Muslim women's contributions to public life are not a past or foreign phenomenon. They are happening now, here, in North America.

The collage as argument: The juxtaposition of images Hajar's sacred geography alongside Ibtihaj Muhammad's fencing uniform, Nadwi's 43-volume encyclopedia alongside Ginella Massa's anchor desk insists on the irreducible plurality of Muslim women's experience across centuries and continents. This anti-essentialist position challenges two reductive moves: the Western tendency to view Muslim women primarily as oppressed, and the conservative tendency to assign them a single fixed role.
